text:
Utah put 12 shots on goal and won. Anaheim put 31 on Sebastian Cossa and lost. That is the box score version, and it undersells how even this game really was.

The shot counts hide shot quality. The Ducks had 61 attempts to Utah's 40, but most of them came from places goalies expect to stop: Anaheim's 2.10 expected goals (the quality of their chances) barely trailed Utah's 2.20, and in our replays of every shot the Mammoth win 51% of the time. Utah made its few looks count. Vincent Trocheck's equalizer late in the first came on a 60% chance, the best of the night by a distance, and answered Leo Carlsson's opener from Cutter Gauthier. Carlsson played only 6:06 in total.

The goal that tilted it was the unlikely one. Andrew Peeke, a defenseman with one shot all night, scored from a 4% chance in the second period, set up by Logan Cooley and Daniil But, and Utah's win chance jumped from 52% to 72%. From there it was Cossa's game. He finished with 29 saves on 31 shots, slightly better than expected, and the stop that mattered most was on Troy Terry midway through the third. He took the first star and added more to Utah's win chances than any skater.

Cooley made it 3-1 with 1:17 left, which stood as the winner after Ian Moore's slap shot with 12 seconds to go, a 1% chance by our numbers, made the final 3-2. Cooley has been at the centre of Utah's week: Gabriel Landeskog was fined for cross-checking him earlier this week against Colorado, and Jack McBain fought Landeskog over it. Utah's Liam O'Brien put the team's position plainly in a Denver Post quote reporter Corey Masisak shared: "If you touch any of our top guys, me and the boys are coming for you."

Anaheim will look at 31 shots and wonder how it got nothing. Our answer: Utah won 30 of 46 faceoffs and gave up volume, but not much more quality than it created.
headline: Mammoth win on 12 shots behind Sebastian Cossa
